title: Tony Schwartz's critical Trump profile preceded their collaboration on The Art of the Deal
description_medium: In 1985 Tony Schwartz wrote a sharply critical New York magazine profile of Donald Trump, focusing on his effort to remove rent-controlled tenants from a building he had bought. Schwartz later approached Trump with the idea for a jointly authored book, The Art of the Deal. The New Yorker’s account of the publishing process describes the project’s 1985 beginnings and the book’s 1987 release.
description_long: Tony Schwartz’s relationship with Donald Trump began in print before the two worked together. In 1985, Schwartz wrote a critical New York magazine cover story about Trump’s attempt to evict rent-controlled tenants from a building he owned on Central Park South, with the aim of converting it to condominiums. Schwartz later came to Trump with a proposal for a book, and they agreed to collaborate on The Art of the Deal. The book was published in 1987, with Schwartz credited as co-author. Schwartz later recalled that Trump admired the critical cover image and treated him as a friend after the story appeared. The contrast between the earlier reporting and the later partnership is documented in Schwartz’s own interview and in the publisher’s recollection of how the book project began. These accounts establish that the article preceded the collaboration, but they do not specify a single date when Trump first hired Schwartz; the better-documented event is the transition from profile subject to book collaborators.
evidence_notes: PBS interview with Schwartz identifies the 1985 New York magazine story, tenant dispute, and Trump’s positive reaction to the cover; New Yorker publisher Peter Osnos recounts the 1985 book pitch and 1987 release. Title now describes the sourced sequence rather than implying an exact hiring date.
corrected_wording: Retitled to center the supported sequence: critical 1985 profile followed by collaboration on The Art of the Deal.

title: Project 2025 proposed changes to technology and media policy, not mass data-retention mandates
description_medium: Project 2025 proposed major changes to technology and media policy, including a more politically directed Federal Trade Commission approach to Big Tech antitrust cases and expanded presidential influence over agencies. Brookings noted that the plan remained vague on AI and did not propose solutions for privacy and safety. The linked coverage does not document a Trump order requiring companies to retain users’ communications, location histories, or browsing data for government access.
description_long: Project 2025 presented a policy program for a possible conservative administration, including proposals affecting technology, media, and communications. Brookings’ analysis describes plans to expand presidential power over agencies and to redirect Federal Trade Commission antitrust enforcement toward what the project’s authors characterize as social and political concerns about Big Tech. The analysis also emphasizes that Project 2025 says little about artificial intelligence policy and does not set out solutions for privacy, safety, or the information ecosystem. Those proposals are different from the claim in the previous description that Trump implemented a comprehensive data-retention system. The Brookings and WIRED links supplied for this entry do not identify a rule compelling companies to retain all communications, browsing records, or location data, do not set a retention period, and do not create blanket government access. They also do not establish the alleged encryption backdoors or warrantless surveillance infrastructure. This entry therefore describes the actual technology-policy discussion in the cited coverage and distinguishes recommendations from implemented mandates.
evidence_notes: Brookings says Project 2025 proposes politically oriented FTC Big Tech antitrust enforcement, agency control shifts, and leaves AI privacy/safety questions vague; supplied sources do not support mandatory data retention, backdoors, or blanket access.
corrected_wording: Replaced unsupported claims of implemented surveillance mandates with a description of Project 2025 technology and media recommendations; title now distinguishes proposals from actual requirements.

title: Donald Trump said in 2002 that he had known Jeffrey Epstein for 15 years
description_medium: In a 2002 New York magazine interview, Donald Trump said he had known Jeffrey Epstein for 15 years. That remark places their acquaintance approximately in the late 1980s, but it does not identify when, where, or how they first met. The timeline’s July 1, 1987 date is a calculation from the retrospective statement, not a documented first encounter.
description_long: Donald Trump’s earliest acquaintance with Jeffrey Epstein is not pinned to a documented first meeting in the sources supplied for this entry. In a 2002 interview with New York magazine, Trump said that he had known Epstein for 15 years. Taken at face value, the remark places their acquaintance around 1987, roughly, rather than on a particular day. The TrumpFile timeline converts that estimate into July 1, 1987, but the interview does not supply that date or describe an initial encounter. Later accounts place the men in overlapping social settings, including a reported 1990 visit by Trump to Epstein’s Palm Beach home, which confirms an association by then but does not resolve when it began. The record is therefore best understood as an approximate acquaintance date derived from Trump’s own retrospective comment. The exact first meeting, including its date and circumstances, remains undocumented in the linked material.
evidence_notes: New York magazine’s 2002 interview is the basis for the 15-year estimate. The timeline’s July 1 date is an arbitrary calendar conversion, not contemporaneous evidence. Later social accounts do not establish a first meeting.
corrected_wording: Retitled from an exact first-meeting claim to the dated, attributable 2002 statement that supports an approximate acquaintance period.
exact_blocker: No linked source identifies the date or circumstances of Trump and Epstein’s first meeting; July 1, 1987 is an inferred placeholder from a retrospective '15 years' statement.

title: FTC asked Justice Department to prosecute Trump over his Bally Manufacturing stake
description_medium: A 1987 report said the Federal Trade Commission asked the Justice Department to prosecute Donald Trump over his use of a “parking agreement” while accumulating a 9.9% stake in Bally Manufacturing. The arrangement involved Bear Stearns and allowed shares to be amassed through a third party. Trump acknowledged using the arrangement but denied it was illegal. The supplied sources do not establish the Justice Department’s response or any prosecution.
description_long: In November 1987, TIME reported that the Federal Trade Commission had asked the Justice Department to prosecute Donald Trump for using a “parking agreement” while building a 9.9% stake in Bally Manufacturing. Under the arrangement described in the report, a corporate raider used a third party, such as an investment bank, to acquire shares in a takeover target without immediately disclosing the accumulation. The article said Trump acknowledged using this type of agreement with Bear Stearns during his Bally share purchases, while denying that the practice was illegal. The reported referral was a request by the FTC, not a finding of guilt or a court judgment. The sources provided with the record do not establish whether the Justice Department filed a case, declined to proceed, or took another action. The entry can describe the FTC’s reported request and Trump’s response, but it should not imply that he was prosecuted or convicted.
evidence_notes: TIME’s contemporaneous report identifies Bally Manufacturing, the 9.9% stake, Bear Stearns, the FTC request, and Trump’s denial of illegality. No disposition is supplied.
corrected_wording: Retitled to identify the target and the FTC’s request, while distinguishing the referral from proof of a violation.
exact_blocker: The linked material does not establish what the Justice Department did in response to the FTC request or whether a prosecution followed.

title: TrumpFile timeline alleges Robert Maxwell obtained Israeli passports for Mogilevich associates
description_medium: A TrumpFile timeline alleges that publisher Robert Maxwell obtained Israeli passports for Russian organized-crime figure Semion Mogilevich and 23 associates in 1988. It further claims Maxwell connected Mogilevich to a Bank of New York account and describes alleged ties involving the KGB and Mossad. These claims rely on secondary accounts cited by the timeline; the supplied material contains no passport or bank records independently confirming the transactions.
description_long: A TrumpFile timeline places an alleged passport arrangement in 1988, claiming that Robert Maxwell obtained Israeli passports for Semion Mogilevich and 23 associates. It also says Maxwell helped Mogilevich establish an account at the Bank of New York and situates the alleged activity within a scheme involving Soviet intelligence and organized crime. The timeline cites Craig Unger’s book *American Kompromat* and other secondary material when discussing Maxwell’s intelligence connections. The claims are serious, but the supplied record does not include passport applications, bank documents, court findings, or contemporaneous reporting that independently confirms the alleged transactions. The timeline’s headline says Maxwell “helps KGB,” while its narrative combines allegations about intelligence contacts, organized crime, and a post-Soviet power plan; those claims should not be treated as established fact merely because they appear together in a later account. The specific 1988 passport and banking allegations remain uncorroborated in the material available for this entry.
evidence_notes: TrumpFile makes the passport, bank-account, and intelligence allegations and cites secondary accounts including Unger. No primary documents or independent contemporaneous substantiation are present in the source packet.
corrected_wording: Changed title to attribute the allegation to TrumpFile and avoid stating a KGB relationship as fact.
exact_blocker: No primary records or independent contemporaneous sources in the supplied materials confirm the claimed passports, Bank of New York account arrangement, or KGB role.
